comparator.name: Bachelor Architecture, Urbanism and Building Sciences
comparator.academicYear: Adopted 2026–2027 ordinary cohort requirements; checked against the completed 7 October audit and current source retrieval on 8 October 2026
comparator.sourceNotes: The current official programme page corroborates the broad Dutch 180-EC bachelor, five prescribed semesters and a minor semester, with 24 required modules in five learning lines. The adopted 2026–2027 regulation and semester schedule, verified in the completed 7 October audit, specify 150 required EC: six design modules ON1–ON4/IOP1–IOP2 at 10 EC (60); six science/skills modules WV1–WV6 at 5 (30); five technology modules TE1–TE5 at 5 (25); four foundations modules GR1–GR4 at 5 (20); three society modules MA1–MA3 at 5 (15). The genuine 30-EC minor completes 180. The existing three year-total placeholders are replaced by the individual coded modules and minor, each counted once in the formal semester/year placement. The final Bachelor Eindproject comprises IOP1, IOP2, TE5 and WV6, totaling 30 within these existing credits; no additional thesis or project credit is appended. Code/learning-line labels are descriptive, not invented catalogue titles. The programme page freshly retrieved on 8 October corroborates the module counts/weights, design/technology/social synthesis and written reflection. Fresh regulation download returned HTTP 502, so its table authority and visual inspection are explicitly carried from the 7 October audit rather than represented as a new retrieval. Reassessment verification on 10 October 2026: the adopted 2026–2027 PDF was successfully retrieved and its Appendix II (p.40) visually checked; it confirms all five learning-line totals and the existing 30-EC BEP aggregation. Current programme and official DigiPedia WV3/WV4 descriptions establish the computational-design/research content used for the UCR assessment. Historical access notes above refer to the earlier correction date.

core: Materials, energy and the life cycle of built environments
Evidence-based spatial research and computational design
adjacent: User needs, housing development and management of shared environments

courses: New Issues in Contemporary Social Theory
trace: introduces markets, public/private decisions and macroeconomic constraints as tools for the documented built-environment management/development direction
analyses public goods, externalities, public spending and redistribution as specific economic problems of shared environmental infrastructure and development
develops research design, sampling and statistical inference for the target’s evidenced empirical spatial research
implements constraint satisfaction, graph search and optimisation as mathematical tools for the documented constraint-based and performance-oriented spatial-design questions
practises data cleaning, visualisation and an empirical data-analysis project, supporting the documented WV4 computational-research method
implements statistical learning and predictive models, supporting the explicitly documented AI-assisted performance/design-analysis direction rather than claiming architectural software training
supplies programming tools for the target’s documented computational-data, simulation and optimisation research
directly studies how human structures, planning and engineering can use natural forces while preserving habitats
studies flood protection, drainage, salinisation, subsidence, land-use decisions and unequal access to water protection in inhabited deltas
studies resource recovery, remediation and circular technologies, supporting the evidenced material-life-cycle direction without claiming construction-material engineering
analyses collective sustainability decisions, interests and policy solutions involving freshwater, energy and climate that constrain built environments
studies Earth processes and natural hazards underlying landscape suitability and risk-aware development
practises GIS and geospatial data integration for soil/water governance and coastal-protection planning
investigates soils and aquifers through fieldwork, laboratory analysis and mapping for geothermal energy, coastal defence and freshwater assessment
studies soil-mineral-water interactions, wastewater treatment and recovery of resources through geochemical modelling
researches geothermal energy, carbon storage and other resource/environmental constraints on sustainable development
establishes planetary-boundary and human-development constraints for environmentally responsible settlement and landscape decisions
studies waves, chemistry and material science as the foundation for advanced material recovery and renewable-system assessment
studies climate impacts on construction and transport and mitigation/adaptation including climate-adaptive spatial planning
evaluates the impacts of products and processes from material extraction to disposal and reuse using hands-on life-cycle analysis
assesses energy-demand patterns and solar, wind and bioenergy solutions with technical and economic analysis for a partner organisation

conducts an externally supported sustainability research project in the Zeeland delta; the broad project remit is a complementary research function, not an architectural studio or a guaranteed building-design assignment
studies institutions, social interaction, race and gender as the social-analysis foundation for assessing whose needs are represented in shared built environments; it is not an urban-design course
practises interviewing, qualitative data interpretation and reflexivity as methods for investigating user needs and experiences in the evidenced people-environment direction
studies civil society, solidarity, trust and migrant inclusion with an organisation-based project, supporting the target’s stakeholder/user dimension without claiming housing or planning practice
investigates ancient settlements, manufacture and material artefacts in relation to social and environmental identities, providing a specific historical perspective on human-made environments
studies Renaissance architecture together with art and Mediterranean exchange, supplying documented historical architectural content at the workbook description scope

alternatives.label: Sustainable built environments & spatial data
alternatives.concept: Approach the built environment through inhabited landscapes, climate-adaptive development, material and energy life cycles, historical settlements and evidence-based spatial/computational research. This is the strongest complete related-fields response; it preserves the absence of the architectural studio, structural and building-physics sequence.
alternatives.labelReason: Environmental systems and resource/energy study dominate, with specific historical-settlement and computational methods; the label does not imply an Architecture degree or complete design formation.
progression: Hard prerequisites, exact six-term availability, 24 unique courses, PPD in year one and at least six level-300 courses passed. Sustainability gateways precede dependent environmental courses; programming precedes optimisation; methods precede advanced empirical/economic work. Earth observation, soils/aquifers and Living with Water are placed in their sole available semester four. Spatial Planning ENSSUST315 and Energy & Sustainability ENSSUST211 are excluded because none of the six cohort terms has an availability mark. Foundations precede resource, energy and community-based advanced work where the fixed timetable permits.

alternatives.label: Sustainable environments, communities & development
alternatives.concept: Retain the material, climate and spatial evidence core while examining user needs, collective decision-making, inclusion and public-economic development of shared environments.
alternatives.labelReason: The completed curriculum replaces algorithmic/data specialisation with substantial social and economic inquiry while retaining the environmental and historical-place core.

alternatives.distinctness: Four courses / 30 EC differ: programming, data-science analysis, machine learning and optimisation are replaced by sociology, contemporary civil-society theory, introductory economics and public economics. These changes implement the evidenced stakeholder/management concept, rather than arbitrary variety.

candidates.label: Construction technology and design across building scales

selection.assessment: Two complete related-fields programmes pass coherence, course-level relevance and distinctness. A separate adaptive-reuse concept does not yield a sufficiently different defensible programme beyond the material-life-cycle and settlement/architectural-history work already included; adding museum or literary courses would not create building transformation practice. The separately assessed construction/scaled-design candidate is not feasible because the workbook lacks architectural studio progression, applied structural mechanics, building physics and construction design. The unavailable Spatial Planning course was assessed but not used. These limitations remain explicit rather than being hidden by complementary sustainability courses.

blocks: The official WV3 description explicitly teaches analysis, simulation and AI-assisted performance optimisation; the UCR course directly teaches constrained optimisation and graph/constraint algorithms. UCR does not supply the module’s full 3D architectural design environment.

The official WV4 computational-methods description explicitly teaches dataset analysis and data generation for built-environment research. UCR data preparation, visualisation and project analysis address that important method but not the full philosophical/writing module.

notes.text: Bouwkunde combines architectural and integrated design studios with structural/building technology, historical foundations and social inquiry. These UCR programmes study related spatial, environmental, computational and community questions, but do not reproduce architectural studio formation, structural design or building physics. The external final project remains distributed across its four credited modules; optional UCR independent research is shown separately.
